name: Maya Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fly in and fly out to a lithium mine way out in the desert, two weeks on and one week off. On site I run a grader, keeping the haul roads smooth so the big trucks don't wreck their tyres, and some days I'm on the water cart spraying the roads to keep the dust down. I'm a year in and still not great at getting a clean finish on the corners, so my supervisor, Dana, follows me in the light vehicle and points. I like the quiet out there, and the stars at night from the camp.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in the city with my sister Inès, who's at university. I'm single. Because I spend half my life at camp with meals paid, I save a lot, probably over a year of pay now, and I've got a small investment flat my parents helped me buy that I rent out. Lithium mines are hiring all over the region, so there's always another camp if this one doesn't work out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the safest one for me, I think. Roads still need fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd mean it. On site there's always talk about the next big thing, and it usually turns out to be a new form to fill in. I'd probably joke about it in the camp mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think my job is safe for years, as long as lithium prices hold. The real risk is the price, because when it dropped two years ago a few mines shut down overnight. That's what I keep an eye on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my swings and finish my grader training properly. I'd keep saving and put a bit more into my investment flat, maybe new kitchen so I can charge more rent. I'd use the chatbot to plan my week off, like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, pretty good about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the lithium price dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camp two hours from ours closed, and some of those workers came to us. When the lithium price fell two years ago, a whole mine near our camp shut in a week, and nobody blamed a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would that kind of drop worry you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but there's always another mine, and I have savings. I'd take a few weeks off and find another camp.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, because the big thing is usually a new form.
I'd **joke about it** in the camp mess.
think: Her job is **safe for years** if lithium prices hold.
The **lithium price** is the real risk, not AI.
do: Put new money into the **investment flat**, maybe a new kitchen.
Keep using the **chatbot** to plan her weeks off.

She uses AI **now and then**, for personal planning.

steps.text: Finish her grader training at the lithium mine
Put a new kitchen in the rental flat to raise rent
Keep saving most of each swing's pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a bit more serious, but it sounds manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work it's probably going to change the office side first, like scheduling and supply orders, and we'll see the robots later. With friends I'd say I'm fine, I work with my hands. I wouldn't say much online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it changes how I'm managed. Software will plan the road work and track every pass I make with the grader. Software that tracks every pass of my grader would know I'm slow on the corners before Dana (my supervisor) ever says it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for more training so I'm not the slowest. I'd try out any new tools the mine brings in, once the others have tested them. And I'd keep my savings steady, maybe hold off on the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, just watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try AI tools at work to get ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once they're proven, yes. I'm not the first to try things, but I'm not the last. If the crew says the new app works, I'll use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the camp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cooks and the cleaners, maybe. If robots take over camp cleaning, those jobs are gone. And the dispatch people.

fieldNote: She sees AI arriving as **management software**, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, then robots three years after. That's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a mess for a while, and the government should help people switch. I'd say that to Inès and to anyone at the camp. I'd still not post much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the grader is hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031. But road grading is simple for a robot, a set path and a set finish. Grading a haul road is a straight line and a flat finish, which is about the easiest thing in the mine to hand to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any big spending and keep the investment flat as a backup. I'd look for a job with more variety, like a mechanic's offsider, so I'm learning a trade before 2031. And I'd keep saving every swing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd need to keep busy so I didn't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in FIFO work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. If I'm retraining, I'd want to be home more. But the money's so good I'd stay as long as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inès?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To finish university, but pick something that needs people in person. She's studying business, so I'd worry for her more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years and then eight for the robots. A bit more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to get ready, and companies should pay for people to retrain. At the camp I'd say it's something to plan for, not panic about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the grader goes around 2034. That gives me years to learn a trade. By 2034 I'd want a real trade ticket in my pocket, not just a grader I'm still slow on the corners with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a heavy-duty mechanic apprenticeship in a couple of years, while still doing FIFO for the money. I'd keep the flat and maybe buy another one. I'd use AI tools a bit more to help study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why another flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because rent comes in whether I have a job or not. It's my backup if mining goes bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being comfortable. FIFO money is easy to get used to. I'd have to push myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the version we can handle, if we start now. At the camp I'd say it's time to think about the future, not just next swing. I'd keep it simple.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm fine. Ten years is enough for me to finish a trade, buy a second flat and still be under 40 when robots grade the haul roads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing FIFO for a few more years, then start an apprenticeship around 2030. I'd keep saving and investing. I might also buy my own place to live, not just to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move back from FIFO?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, in a few years. I'd want a normal life, maybe a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not knowing what jobs will be safe. A trade feels safe now, but I can't be sure.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because grading is too easy to automate and I wouldn't have a trade yet. What would help is the company paying for apprenticeships while we work. I've got a year of pay saved, but what I really need is a trade nobody can automate by 2031.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about FIFO. The money is good, but it makes it hard to plan a normal life. That affects how I'd react to any of this.

headlineQuote: I've got a year of pay saved, but what I really need is a trade nobody can automate by 2031.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old** FIFO grader operator at a remote lithium mine.
She shares a flat with her sister Inès and has **over a year saved** plus a rental flat.
She tries tools **once proven** and uses AI now and then for planning.
She sees grading as **easy to automate**, so plans a trade.
She's **calm** in the plateau and **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because grading would go before she had a trade.
